report:
### Conclusion
**No**, routine knee arthroscopy (joint endoscopy)—such as arthroscopic lavage or debridement—is not effective for treating osteoarthritis (OA) of the knee joint compared to non-surgical treatments or placebo.

### Evidence Behind the Answer
Multiple high-quality studies and clinical practice guidelines confirm that arthroscopy provides no significant advantage in pain relief or functional improvement for knee OA:

1. **No Superiority Over Placebo**: A landmark placebo-controlled randomized controlled trial (RCT) led by Moseley et al. (2002) demonstrated that patients undergoing arthroscopic debridement or lavage experienced no greater relief in pain or joint function than those receiving a sham (placebo) procedure (https://www.aetna.com/cpb/medical/data/600_699/0673.html).
2. **No Added Benefit Over Physical/Medical Therapy**: A pivotal 2008 RCT by Kirkley et al. showed that adding arthroscopic surgery to optimized medical and physical therapy produced no additional benefits in physical function, stiffness, or pain (https://archive.connect.h1.co/article/1121766/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4010873/).
3. **Clinical Guidelines**: Major orthopaedic bodies, including the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS), advise against performing arthroscopic debridement or lavage for patients with primary knee osteoarthritis (https://www.aetna.com/cpb/medical/data/600_699/0673.html). 

Given these findings, standard medical guidelines support conservative management—such as structured physical therapy, exercise, and medication—over arthroscopic surgery for managing knee osteoarthritis (https://kpjmd.com/ask/is-arthroscopic-surgery-effective-knee-osteoarthritis/).
